evals.prompt:
把下面这篇技术文章翻成中文，术语前后保持一致：

Kubernetes schedules Pods onto Nodes based on resource requests. A Pod's request is the amount of CPU and memory the scheduler reserves for it, while its limit is the maximum it may consume. If a container exceeds its memory limit, it is OOM-killed; if it exceeds its CPU limit, it is throttled rather than killed.

Requests also drive Quality of Service (QoS) classes. When every container in a Pod sets requests equal to limits, the Pod is Guaranteed. When at least one request is set but the Pod is not Guaranteed, it is Burstable. Pods with no requests or limits at all are BestEffort, and they are the first to be evicted under node pressure.

Eviction is distinct from preemption. Eviction happens when a Node runs low on memory or disk, and the kubelet terminates Pods to reclaim resources, starting with BestEffort. Preemption happens at scheduling time: a pending high-priority Pod may cause the scheduler to remove lower-priority Pods so that it can fit.

In practice, set requests close to observed usage and leave headroom in limits. Over-generous requests waste capacity because the scheduler reserves resources that are never used; requests that are too small lead to noisy-neighbour problems and unexpected evictions. Revisit requests regularly, because workloads drift.

Finally, remember that throttling is invisible to most dashboards. A service that looks healthy at 40% average CPU can still suffer latency spikes if it is throttled during bursts. Monitor the container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total metric alongside utilisation.

# Nimbus Distributed Cache: Design Document

## 1. Overview

This document describes the design of Nimbus, a distributed cache that sits between our application tier and the primary database. Nimbus stores frequently read objects in memory so that most requests never reach the database. The cache is organised into shards, and every shard has one leader and two replicas. Clients locate a shard by applying consistent hashing to the cache key.

The rest of this document explains how keys are placed, how writes propagate, how entries expire, and how the system behaves under failure. Section 4 covers the write policies in detail, and Section 7 describes the eviction policy. Readers who only need operational guidance can skip directly to Section 10.

Throughout the document we use the term "cache entry" for a key together with its value and metadata, and "backing store" for the primary database. A cache hit means the entry was found in Nimbus; a cache miss means the client had to read from the backing store.

## 2. Goals and Non-Goals

The primary goal of Nimbus is to keep read latency at the 99th percentile below five milliseconds for cached keys. A secondary goal is to reduce load on the backing store by at least eighty percent during peak traffic. We also want the cache to tolerate the loss of any single node without a visible increase in error rates.

Nimbus is not a database. It does not guarantee durability, and any cache entry may disappear at any time because of eviction, expiry, or node failure. Applications must always be able to rebuild an entry from the backing store. Nimbus also does not provide multi-key transactions; each operation affects exactly one cache key.

Strong consistency between the cache and the backing store is explicitly a non-goal. We aim for bounded staleness instead: under normal operation, a cache entry should never be more than the configured TTL out of date, and Section 5 explains how invalidation shortens that window further.

## 3. Key Placement

Each cache key is hashed onto a ring of virtual nodes. We use consistent hashing so that adding or removing a shard only moves a small fraction of keys. Every physical shard owns two hundred virtual nodes, which smooths out the distribution and prevents any single shard from receiving a disproportionate share of traffic.

When a client starts, it downloads the current ring layout from the configuration service and caches it locally. If a client sends a request to the wrong shard, for example because the ring changed after the client last refreshed its layout, the shard replies with a redirect that contains the new owner. The client then updates its local ring and retries.

Hot keys are a known weakness of consistent hashing. A single extremely popular cache key will always map to the same shard, no matter how many virtual nodes we add. Section 8 describes how Nimbus detects hot keys and spreads their load across replicas.

## 4. Write Policies

Nimbus supports two write policies: write-through and write-back. Under write-through, the client writes to the backing store first and then updates the cache entry. The write is acknowledged only after both steps succeed. Write-through is simple and safe, but it adds the latency of the backing store to every write.

Under write-back, the client writes only to the cache, and the shard leader flushes dirty cache entries to the backing store asynchronously. Write-back gives much lower write latency, but a leader crash before a flush can lose recent writes. For this reason write-back is only enabled for data that the application can afford to lose, such as view counters and session hints.

Both write policies replicate the updated cache entry from the leader to its replicas. The leader acknowledges a write once at least one replica has confirmed it. If neither replica responds within the replication timeout, the leader marks the shard as degraded and continues accepting writes, as described in Section 9.

## 5. Expiry and Invalidation

Every cache entry has a TTL, which is the maximum time it may live in the cache. The default TTL is ten minutes, but applications may set a shorter or longer TTL per key. When the TTL elapses, the entry is treated as a cache miss on the next read, and the client reloads it from the backing store.

TTL alone is not enough for data that changes frequently. When a row in the backing store is updated, the database emits a change event, and an invalidation worker deletes the corresponding cache key from Nimbus. Invalidation usually completes within a few hundred milliseconds, which keeps staleness far below the TTL.

Invalidation messages can be lost, delayed, or reordered. To protect against a delayed invalidation removing a newer value, each cache entry carries a version number taken from the backing store. An invalidation only deletes the entry if its version is less than or equal to the version in the message.

## 6. Read Path

A read begins with the client hashing the cache key and sending the request to the shard leader or, for keys marked as read-mostly, to a randomly chosen replica. If the entry exists and its TTL has not elapsed, the shard returns it immediately. This is the cache hit path, and it accounts for roughly ninety-five percent of requests in production.

On a cache miss, the client reads the value from the backing store and then populates the cache. To avoid a cache stampede, where thousands of clients miss on the same key at the same moment and all query the backing store, Nimbus uses request coalescing. The first client to miss acquires a short lease on the key; other clients that miss while the lease is held wait for the first client to populate the entry instead of querying the backing store themselves.

Leases expire after two seconds. If the lease holder crashes, another client will acquire a new lease once the old one expires, so a single failure cannot block a key indefinitely.

## 7. Eviction Policy

Each shard has a fixed memory budget. When memory usage reaches ninety percent of the budget, the shard begins eviction, removing cache entries until usage falls below eighty percent. Nimbus uses an approximate least-recently-used eviction policy: the shard samples a small set of entries and evicts the one that was accessed least recently.

Eviction is independent of TTL. An entry may be evicted long before its TTL elapses if the shard is under memory pressure, and an entry that is never evicted will still expire when its TTL elapses. Applications must therefore treat every read as a potential cache miss, as stated in Section 2.

Entries written under the write-back policy are never evicted while they are dirty. The shard first flushes a dirty entry to the backing store and only then makes it eligible for eviction. This prevents eviction from silently discarding writes that have not yet reached the backing store.

## 8. Hot Key Mitigation

Every shard tracks request rates per cache key using a lightweight sketch. When the rate for a single key exceeds a configurable threshold, the shard marks it as a hot key and publishes this flag to clients through the configuration service.

Clients that see the hot key flag spread reads for that key across the leader and both replicas instead of sending them only to the leader. For extremely hot keys, clients may also keep a short-lived local copy for up to one second. This local copy is not covered by invalidation, so it is only used for keys whose owners have explicitly opted in.

Hot key detection works together with consistent hashing rather than replacing it. The key still belongs to exactly one shard; only the distribution of reads across that shard's leader and replicas changes.

## 9. Failure Handling

If a shard leader fails, its replicas detect the failure through missed heartbeats and elect a new leader. During the election, which normally takes less than three seconds, writes to that shard are rejected and reads are served by the replicas. Entries written under the write-back policy that were not yet flushed may be lost, as noted in Section 4.

If a replica fails, the leader continues to operate with the remaining replica and the shard is marked as degraded. A degraded shard still serves traffic, but the operations team is alerted, and a replacement replica is provisioned automatically. The new replica copies the current cache entries from the leader before it begins serving reads.

If an entire availability zone fails, consistent hashing ensures that only the shards whose leaders lived in that zone are affected. Their replicas in other zones take over, and the rest of the ring is unchanged.

## 10. Operational Guidance

Operators should watch four metrics: hit ratio, eviction rate, replication lag, and hot key count. A falling hit ratio usually means the working set has outgrown the memory budget, and the fix is to add shards. A rising eviction rate is an early warning of the same problem.

Replication lag measures how far replicas trail the leader. Sustained lag above one second suggests network congestion or an overloaded leader. A rising hot key count often follows a product launch or a marketing campaign and usually resolves on its own, but operators should confirm that clients are spreading reads correctly.

To add capacity, register the new shard with the configuration service. Consistent hashing will move roughly one shard's worth of keys to the new node. The moved keys will experience a brief period of cache misses until they are repopulated from the backing store.

The following snippet shows how a service configures its client:

```yaml
# Nimbus client configuration
nimbus:
  write_policy: write-through   # use write-back only for loss-tolerant data
  default_ttl: 600s             # TTL for cache entries without an explicit value
  read_from_replicas: true      # spread reads for hot keys
  lease_timeout: 2s             # request coalescing lease, see Section 6
```

## 11. Security

All traffic between clients and shards is encrypted with mutual TLS. Each service receives its own client certificate, and shards reject connections from services that are not on the allow-list for a given key prefix. This prevents one team's service from reading another team's cache entries.

Cache entries are stored in memory without additional encryption, because the hosts are already protected by full-disk encryption and strict access controls. Sensitive values such as authentication tokens should not be placed in Nimbus at all; they belong in the dedicated secrets service.

Audit logs record every configuration change, every hot key flag, and every manual invalidation issued by an operator. The logs are retained for ninety days.

## 12. Testing and Rollout

Before Nimbus serves production traffic, every release runs through three stages of testing. Unit tests cover the eviction policy, the TTL logic, and the version checks used by invalidation. Integration tests start a small ring of shards, kill leaders and replicas at random, and verify that no acknowledged write-through update is lost and that the cache never returns an entry older than its TTL.

The third stage is a shadow deployment. A copy of production read traffic is sent to the new release, and its responses are compared with those of the current release. Any difference in hit ratio larger than one percentage point, or any increase in cache stampede events, blocks the rollout until the cause is understood.

Rollout itself proceeds one availability zone at a time. Because consistent hashing keeps most keys on their existing shards, upgrading a zone causes only a short burst of cache misses. Operators monitor the four metrics listed in Section 10 and pause the rollout if replication lag or the hot key count rises unexpectedly.

If a release must be rolled back, operators revert the shards in the reverse order. Entries written under the write-back policy are flushed to the backing store before each shard restarts, so a rollback never discards dirty cache entries.

## 13. Glossary

Backing store: the primary database that holds the authoritative copy of every value.

Cache entry: a cache key together with its value, version number, and TTL.

Consistent hashing: the placement scheme that maps each cache key to a shard while minimising movement when shards change.

Eviction: removal of a cache entry to free memory, independent of its TTL.

Hot key: a cache key whose request rate exceeds the configured threshold.

Invalidation: deletion of a cache entry in response to a change in the backing store.

Write-back and write-through: the two write policies described in Section 4.
